newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary TV channels up for grabs, but price unclear.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary TV channels up for grabs, but price unclear.

text.p: Investors are lining up for chunks of Hungary's potentially lucrative television market, though no one knows the price of the two channels on offer.

"The large number of factors that have to be considered mean it will be very difficult to set the concession fees," said Judit Kormendy-Ekes of the national radio and television regulatory body, Orszagos Radio es Televizio Testulet (ORTT).
Hungary's media law, passed last December after four years of bitter political dispute, was at the time considered a milestone in the country's media history.
It opened the way for the privatisation of a television market that attracted 16 billion forints ($100.8 million) worth of advertisers' money in the first half of 1996.
National television's presently state-owned second channel and a third, which theoretically is nationwide but at the moment is unused, are up for grabs.
Only consortia are expected to bid and no single company is allowed to have more than a 49 percent stake, while Hungarians have to hold a minimum of 26 percent.
A FOREIGN BIDDER
Luxembourg's CLT, which recently merged with Germany's Bertelsmann, is one international media giant to express interest.
"We want to bid for a 49 percent stake in one of the national terrestrial channels," said John Harrington of CLT Multimedia.
However, the involvement of only loosely interconnected ministries, government agencies and broadcast providers makes planning ahead difficult, if not impossible, he said.
"We do not know how much the concession fee will be, how much we are expected to pay Antenna Hungaria, and what the public service requirements would be," Harrington said.

State-owned broadcaster Antenna Hungaria, which handles all transmission, is reported to have debts of more than three billion forints, mainly as a result of arrears in transmission fee payments from state-owned radio and TV channels.
Despite uncertainties, CLT, which operates the RTL channels and is about to start television stations in Poland and Finland, has some outlines of a business plan.
"We expect to start making a profit within two to three years and have our investment back within five to six years," Harrington said.
The concessions will run for 10 years plus a possible additional five.
A DOMESTIC BIDDER
"We would be interested in one of the terrestrial channels, although this is an outdated technology," said Andras Feuer, director general of commercial station TV3.
He added that national television's second channel has the advantage of an existing audience.
"If a concession holder were to start broadcasting on this channel from one day to the next he would have an instant audience," Feuer said.
"On the other hand, this headway is likely to be reflected in the concession fee, so the overall gain might not be too significant."
He also said the political considerations which shaped the media law are rather different from commercial ones.
"For the politicians, one viewer is as good as the other, because they can all cast their votes. For a commercial station, viewers' importance is proportional to their purchasing power," Feuer said.
He did not expect Antenna Hungaria to maintain its monopoly over broadcasting for much longer.
LURE FOR INVESTORS IS ADVERTISING
The bait for investors is a maximum six minutes per hour advertising time.

In 1995, official TV advertising expenditure in Hungary was 26 billion forints, but the actual amount spent on publicity, taking into account sponsorship and advertising disguised as arts patronage could be as much as 20 percent higher, Feuer said.
Overall, advertising expenditure dropped by eight percent in 1995 compared with the previous year, but for 1996 specialists forecast a modest one to 1.5 percent real-term growth.
However, a potential advertising market, virtually nonexistent for the time, could open new sources of revenue.

"Most advertisers either go for national, or local campaigns, while regional television stations are left out. The big question is whether advertising companies could fill in this middle-market," Feuer said.
While allowing 10 percent of broadcast time to advertising, the downside of the law for commercial stations is that it also stipulates public service programming requirements.
Such programmes will have to account for 25 percent of total airtime, and at least 35 percent of own programmes have to be of Hungarian production.
This legal requirement could be a boon for independent production companies, Harrington said.
"We plan to work a lot with independent production companies, much like Britain's Channel Four did, which in a very short time created an independent industry," he said.
The bulk of a mandatory news programme has to be done in-house, but Harrington does not regard this as a drawback.
"News is important, as there is demand and it can also draw audience," he said.
But the biggest asset is western television expertise.

There is no official deadline for the publication of the tenders, but they are expected to appear around the end of November. Adding the application, winners' announcement and broadcast deadlines, this would amount to national commercial channels going live next summer. ($1=158.68 Forint)
